This tutorial covers the design of large software systems: services that must stay fast, correct and available while
their load, their data and their failures grow. It starts with the design process and with estimates of load, storage
and availability, then follows a request through the web stack and measures performance with queueing theory. It moves
through storage and databases, replication and partitioning, consistency and consensus, caching, messaging, distributed
transactions, and batch and stream processing. It ends with architecture styles, reliability and operations, and case
studies of infrastructure services and applications.

Each chapter sets out definitions and results, works through examples, and gives exercises to try. Results with a
published proof, such as Little's law, quorum intersection or the CAP theorem, are stated as theorems and proved, and
design patterns are stated as definitions. Quantitative examples and solutions are computed by code that runs, and
architectures are drawn as diagrams from their sources. The probability comes from
[Fundamentals of Mathematics for Physicists](../fundamentals-of-mathematics-for-physicists/index.qmd), and some
random processes and network models from [Complexity Science](../complexity-science/index.qmd).

::: {.start-reading}
The chapters are listed in reading order in the sidebar, followed by the [glossary](glossary/index.qmd). [Start with the notation →](notation/index.qmd)
:::

## Prerequisites

The chapters assume programming experience and the following chapters of the other tutorials, and link to them where a
result is used:

- [Probability](../fundamentals-of-mathematics-for-physicists/probability/index.qmd): independence, random variables,
  the exponential and Poisson distributions and limit theorems, for availability, queueing, hashing and sketches.
- [Sets, relations and topology](../fundamentals-of-mathematics-for-physicists/sets-relations-topology/index.qmd):
  relations and orders, for happens-before and consistency models.

## Software

Every computation runs in plain Python 3.12, with [SimPy](https://simpy.readthedocs.io) 4.1.2 for discrete-event
simulation and the standard library's `sqlite3` for storage and indexing. Simulations use fixed seeds, so the recorded
outputs on the pages can be reproduced. Code that would need a live service, such as a database server, a message
broker or a load generator, is shown as illustrative code: it is marked as not run, and it has no recorded output.

Main libraries:

- [SimPy](https://simpy.readthedocs.io) 4.1.2: discrete-event simulation, for queues, retries, replication and
  consensus protocols.
- [`sqlite3`](https://docs.python.org/3/library/sqlite3.html): the SQLite database in the standard library, for
  schemas, indexes, transactions and full-text search.

Other libraries:

- [NumPy](https://numpy.org): arrays, random numbers and percentiles.
- [matplotlib](https://matplotlib.org): plots of the simulations.
- [D2](https://d2lang.com) v0.9.0: the language in which the architecture, data-flow and sequence diagrams are
  written.

The Python libraries are installed, at the versions the pages were computed with, into the `.venv-systems`
environment by one command run from the root of the [repository](https://github.com/georgedouzas/tutorials) (Python
3.12 and [uv](https://docs.astral.sh/uv/) required):

```bash
uv venv --python 3.12 .venv-systems && uv pip install --python .venv-systems/bin/python -r system-design/requirements.lock
```

The diagrams are regenerated with D2 v0.9.0 on the `PATH`.

This tutorial has its own [glossary](glossary/index.qmd).
